title: Essential English · Julia
topic: To Pick Up & Drop Off / Pronoun Position in Phrasal Verbs

sections.title: 1. Pick Up & Drop Off — Meaning
sections.content:
Two opposite phrasal verbs for collecting and leaving people (or things).

| Phrasal verb | Spanish | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Pick up** | Recoger / ir a buscar | *I'll pick you up at the airport.* |
| **Drop off** | Dejar (a alguien en un sitio) | *He dropped her off at the hotel.* |

> **Drop** alone = dejar caer (accidentally). **Drop off** = leave someone somewhere on purpose.

> In English, if a phrasal verb option exists, prefer it over the plain verb — especially in spoken English.

sections.title: 2. Separable Phrasal Verbs & the Pronoun Rule  ★ Main topic
sections.content:
**Pick up** and **drop off** are both separable — the object can go in two positions.

### When the object is a noun → two options (both correct)

| Position | Example |
|---|---|
| Noun **after** the preposition | She will pick up **Peter** at the airport. |
| Noun **between** verb and preposition | She will pick **Peter** up at the airport. |

---

### When the object is a pronoun → only ONE option

The pronoun **must** go between the verb and the preposition. No exceptions.

| Correct | Wrong |
|---|---|
| She will pick **him** up at the airport. ✓ | ~~She will pick up him at the airport.~~ ✗ |
| He dropped **her** off at the hotel. ✓ | ~~He dropped off her at the hotel.~~ ✗ |
| She picks **them** up from school. ✓ | ~~She picks up them from school.~~ ✗ |

---

### Non-separable phrasal verbs (for reference)

Non-separable phrasal verbs cannot have anything placed between verb and preposition — not even a pronoun.

- *listen to it* ✓ · ~~listen it to~~ ✗

---

### The 'chunk' rule

When using a pronoun, treat the three words as one unit — say them connected:

> **pick him up** · **drop her off** · **picks them up**

Avoid leaving the preposition hanging: ~~pick him ... up~~ sounds unnatural.

sections.title: 3. Practice: The Three Variations
sections.content:
For each question, give three answers: noun at end → noun in middle → pronoun in middle.

---

**Will she pick up Peter at the airport?**
1. Yes, she will pick up Peter at the airport.
2. Yes, she will pick Peter up at the airport.
3. Yes, she will pick **him** up at the airport.

---

**Did he drop off his boss at the hotel?**
1. Yes, he dropped off his boss at the hotel.
2. Yes, he dropped his boss off at the hotel.
3. Yes, he dropped **him/her** off at the hotel.

> *his boss* — the possessive *his* refers to the subject, not the gender of *boss*. Boss can be male or female, so the pronoun can be *him* or *her*.

---

**Does she pick up the children from school?**
1. Yes, she picks up the children from school.
2. Yes, she picks the children up from school.
3. Yes, she picks **them** up from school.

> Third person -s goes on the verb only — never on the preposition: *she picks up* ✓ · ~~she picks ups~~ ✗

---

**Can you drop me off at the station?**
→ Already a pronoun, so only one option:
Yes, I can drop **you** off at the station.

---

**Will you drop off your colleagues at the office?**
1. Yes, I will drop off my colleagues at the office.
2. Yes, I will drop my colleagues off at the office.
3. Yes, I will drop **them** off at the office.

---

**Did Susan pick up her mother at the hospital?**
1. Yes, Susan picked up her mother at the hospital.
2. Yes, Susan picked her mother up at the hospital.
3. Yes, Susan picked **her** up at the hospital.

sections.title: 4. Vocabulary & Pronunciation Notes
sections.content:
### Vocabulary

| Word / phrase | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Colleagues** | British English = compañeros de trabajo. American = *co-workers*. |
| **Fellas** | Very American informal for 'guys'. Not rude. Used alone: *hi fellas.* |
| **Fellow** | Used as adjective: *fellow students* = compañeros de clase. |
| **Mates** | British informal for friends/companions (*fellas* equivalent). |
| **A chunk** | A connected group of words: *pick him up* is one chunk. |
| **From/at school** | Both work: *pick up the children from school / at school.* |

---

### Pronunciation: -ed endings

**Dropped** — regular verb, double *p* in writing. Pronounce as one syllable: **dropped** /drɒpt/

- Say the *d* and *t* as one blended sound at the end — not two syllables.
- ~~drop-it~~ ✗ → **dropped** ✓

**Picked** — one syllable: /pɪkt/ — same principle.

---

### Hotel — stress

Stress falls on the **second** syllable: *ho-**TEL*** — not ~~**HO**-tel~~.

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
**Direct & Indirect Object Pronouns**

When a pronoun replaces the object, the word order changes — the preposition **to** is required:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Explícamelo una vez más | Explain it to me one more time *(not "explain me it")* |
| Kyle le está dando el libro a Pepe | Kyle is giving Pepe the book → He is giving **it** to **him** |

---

**Translation practice from class**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Fue mucho más fácil que la última vez | It was much easier than the last time |
| ¿Cuánto tardó? | How long did it take you? *(subject = "it")* |
| Él estaba mejor preparado que yo | He was better prepared than me / than I was |
| Vino el fontanero para mirarlo | The plumber came to look at it |
| Se estaban quejando de la falta de un plan concreto | They were complaining about the lack of a concrete plan |
| Pero vieron esto, ¿no? | But they saw this, **didn't they**? |

> **Vocabulary note:** *plumber* has a **silent B** — another example: *crumbs*.

sections.title: 2. Question Tags
sections.content:
Take the **auxiliary verb**, flip it (affirmative → negative or negative → affirmative), then repeat the subject pronoun.

| Sentence | Tag |
|---|---|
| It is important… | …isn't it? |
| You like coffee… | …don't you? |
| He likes fish… | …doesn't he? |
| He was here yesterday… | …wasn't he? |
| They can't fix it… | …can they? |
| But they saw this… | …didn't they? |

> With the verb **to be**, it acts as its own auxiliary — no extra verb needed.
>
> In Canadian English, people informally say **"eh?"** instead of a proper tag (not standard, but common).

sections.title: 3. Picture Vocabulary
sections.content:

| Sunrise/sunset scene | The sun is **rising** / **setting** over the desert |
| Crowd entering a store | They're **rushing into** the store / They're **crashing the door** *(Black Friday)* |
| People in the rain | They're **taking shelter** under a palm leaf |
| Person with gift | She/he is **wrapping a gift** / **wrapping a present** · **wrapping paper** |

**Extra vocabulary:**
- **A sale / on sale** — something sold at a reduced price
- **Door crash deal** — a special offer only for the first people through the door (Black Friday term)
- **Mixed reviews** — some people liked it, some didn't *(taquilla = box office)*

sections.title: 4. Comparatives with as…as  ★ Main topic
sections.content:
### Basic structure: **as … as** / **not as … as**

*tan … como / no tan … como*

- Valencia is **not as big as** Madrid
- I'm **not as tall as** my brother
- English is **not as difficult as** Chinese

---

### 1. Not quite as … as — *small gap, close comparison*

> Implies the two things are **almost the same** but one falls slightly short.

- It's **not quite as** salty **as** last time *(casi igual de salado)*
- The museum wasn't **quite as** interesting as we hoped
- The exam wasn't **quite as** difficult as I thought it would be
- Barcelona isn't **quite as** big as Madrid
- My house isn't **quite as** big as my brother's
- The film is **not quite as** good as the book
- His second book is **not quite as** interesting as the first
- Málaga's beaches aren't **quite as** long as Cádiz's

---

### 2. Not nearly as … as — *large gap, big difference*

> Implies there is a **significant** difference — one thing is much less than the other.

- I'm **not nearly as** fast as Usain Bolt *(con mucha diferencia)*
- Trujillo isn't **nearly as** big as Madrid
- This cover isn't **nearly as** good as the Beatles original
- His desk isn't **nearly as** untidy as hers
- The film isn't **nearly as** good as the book
- My hometown is **not nearly as** crowded as Madrid
- It doesn't have **nearly as much** traffic as Madrid *(countable/uncountable applies: as much / as many)*

---

### Quick comparison

| Expression | Spanish equivalent | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| not quite as … as | no tan … como *(casi)* | Small — almost equal |
| not nearly as … as | ni con mucho tan … como | Large — clearly less |

---

### 3. Just about as … as — *almost equal, barely reaches*

> Like saying *casi* — it's right there, very close.

- I'm **just about as** good as him at tennis *(casi tan bueno como él)*
- My brother is taller but I'm **just about as** tall
- My mother's cooking is **just about** the best in the world
- My grandmother was **just about** the most cheerful person I've ever known
- It's **just about** the best burger in town

---

### 4. Just about to — *on the verge of doing something*

> Means *a punto de hacer algo* — you were very close to doing it but didn't.

- I was **just about to** call you *(a punto de llamarte)*
- He was **just about to** open the window when it started pouring
- That's what I was **just about to** say
- I was **just about to** go out when you called me
- I was just about to warn you when the ceiling fell

> **Note:** this is different from *just about + adjective* above — same words, different meaning depending on context.

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Según él, deberías haberlo hecho | According to him, you should have done it |
| Hay un viejo dicho sobre ese tema | There's an old saying about that subject |
| En cuanto a mí se refiere | As far as I'm concerned *(you can do whatever you want)* |
| Si fueras un poco más optimista | If you were a little more optimistic |
| Soy pesimista por naturaleza | I'm a pessimist / I'm pessimistic |
| Todos a favor del plan que levanten la mano | All in favor of the plan, raise your hand |
| Se fue por el desagüe | It went down the drain |
| ¿Qué harás cuando te jubiles? | What will you do when you retire? |
| Haré un viaje alrededor del mundo | I'll take a trip around the world |

> **Vocabulary:** *to gurgle* — the sound water makes going down a drain. Informal: *it went down the gurgler.*

> **Trip vs. Travel:** *travel* is the verb (*we traveled to Rome*); *trip* is the noun and needs another verb — *to take a trip, to go on a trip* (*not* ~~to trip to Rome~~).

sections.title: 2. What does he look like? / How does he look? / What is he like?  ★ Main topic
sections.content:
Two dimensions to consider: **physical appearance** vs. **personality**, and **permanent/fact** vs. **temporary/opinion**.

| | Physical appearance | Personality |
|---|---|---|
| Permanent / fact | **What does he look like?** | **What is he like?** |
| Temporary / opinion | **How does he look?** | **How is he?** |

---

### Physical appearance

**What does he look like?** — permanent, factual description

- What does your brother look like? → *He's tall and has gray hair.*
- What did your grandfather look like? → *He was tall and strong and had gray hair.*
- What will the city look like after the renovations?
- What does Santa Claus look like? → *He's fat and wears a red suit.*

> Answer with **to be** or **to have** — never *he looks like tall* ✗

**How does he look?** — temporary, invites an opinion

- How did he look when you saw him? → *He looked tired / ill / different.*
- How does she look? → *She looks much healthier than before.*

---

### Personality

**What is he like?** — permanent character traits

- What is your brother like? → *He's hardworking, stubborn, and very generous.*
- What was your grandmother like? → *She was strict but loving.*

**How is he?** — temporary mood or state

- How is your neighbour these days? → *He's much more relaxed than he used to be.*
- How was John when you saw him? → *He was in a great mood.*

---

> **Rule of thumb:** *What* asks for facts/descriptions. *How* asks for opinion or current state. *Like* = permanent. No *like* = temporary.

sections.title: 3. Negative Comparisons: not as many / not as much
sections.content:
Convert **fewer / less** sentences into **not as many / not as much**.

| Type | Direct comparison | Negative comparison |
|---|---|---|
| Countable | There are **fewer** horses in Portugal than in Spain. | There are **not as many** horses in Portugal **as** in Spain. |
| Uncountable | There is **less** water in Jordan than in Canada. | There is **not as much** water in Jordan **as** in Canada. |
| Countable | There are **fewer** languages spoken in Finland than in Africa. | There are **not as many** languages spoken in Finland **as** in Africa. |
| Uncountable | There is **less** sand in Andorra than in Egypt. | There is **not as much** sand in Andorra **as** in Egypt. |
| Countable | There are **fewer** olive trees in Galicia than in Andalusia. | There are **not as many** olive trees in Galicia **as** in Andalusia. |

> The negative form (*there isn't as much / there aren't as many*) is very common in natural speech — more so than the positive *there is as much*. Worth mastering.

**Key:** *as many* = countable (fewer ↔ not as many) · *as much* = uncountable (less ↔ not as much)

sections.title: 4. Grammar Notes
sections.content:
### Noun vs. adjective: pessimist / pessimistic

| Form | Example | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Noun | I'm **a pessimist** | Needs the article |
| Adjective | I'm **pessimistic** | No article |
| Adjective + noun | I'm **a pessimistic person** | Article goes with the noun |

---

### Raise vs. Rise

| Verb | Type | Forms | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Raise** | Transitive (needs object) | raise / raised / raised | I am **raising** my hand. The government **raises** taxes. |
| **Rise** | Intransitive (no object) | rise / **rose** / **risen** | My hand is **rising**. Taxes **rise**. |

> *I raise the phone → the phone rises.* Same event, two verbs depending on whether there is a subject performing the action.

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up: Past Continuous
sections.content:
Used for actions **in progress** when something else happened (interruption) or for **simultaneous** past actions.

Structure: **was/were + verb-ing**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Qué pasó cuando venías aquí? | What happened when you were coming here? |
| Le vi cuando iba a clase | I saw him when he was going to class |
| ¿Qué hacías cuando les viste? | What were you doing when you saw them? |
| ¿A dónde ibas cuando tuviste el accidente? | Where were you going when you had the accident? |
| Bajaba de su coche cuando la bomba estalló | He was getting out of his car when the bomb went off |
| Pensaba en ti cuando me llamaste | I was thinking about you when you called me |
| Cuando me di cuenta del error, ya se iba | When I realized my mistake, he was already leaving |

> **“What did it happen?”** ✗ — When asking for the **subject**, no auxiliary is needed: **“What happened?”** ✓

---

### By the time

*Para cuando* — one thing finished before the other was complete.

- **By the time** I realized my mistake, he was already leaving.
- **By the time** the bus came, we were already late.
- **By the time** our flight arrived, the taxis had already gone.

sections.title: 2. Phrasal Verbs: Get & Blow
sections.content:
### Get into / Get out of — enclosed spaces

Use with **cars, taxis, elevators**:

- **Get into** the car · **Get out of** the car
- **Get into** a taxi · **Get out of** an elevator

### Get on / Get off — large vehicles

Use with **buses, planes, trains**:

- **Get on** the bus · **Get off** the bus
- **Get on** the plane · **Get off** the train

> Things you **get into**, you **get out of**. Things you **get on**, you **get off**.

---

### Blow / Go Off / Put Out

| Expression | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| The bomb **went off** | La bomba estalló | *The bomb went off at midnight.* |
| The building **blew up** | El edificio voló por los aires | *The explosion blew up the building.* |
| **Blow out** a candle | Apagar soplando | *Blow out your birthday candles.* |
| **Put out** a fire | Apagar un incendio | *Firefighters put out the fire.* |

> A bomb **goes off**. A building **blows up**. Candles are **blown out**. Fires are **put out**.

sections.title: 3. Think About / Think Of / Think Up
sections.content:
Three related but distinct expressions:

| Expression | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Think about** | Pasar un rato con algo en la cabeza | *I was thinking about you / about hamburgers.* |
| **Think of** | In the middle — slight implication of invention | *I thought of a solution last night while washing the dishes.* |
| **Think up** | Pure invention / idear | *We need to think up a new recipe for the greatest burger ever.* |

> **Think about** = just having something in your mind, no invention implied.
>
> **Think up** = purely creative — *we need to think up a plan.*
>
> **Think of** = somewhere in between; the idea *appeared* — *I can’t think of the word right now.*

sections.title: 4. Notice vs. Realize
sections.content:
| Expression | Spanish | Type |
|---|---|---|
| **To notice** | Fijarse — con los sentidos | Sensory awareness — less cerebral |
| **To realize** | Darse cuenta | Mental processing — more cerebral |

**Example sequence:**
> *I noticed a strange smell* → sensory, external
> *Then I realized my neighbor was smoking.* → mental processing, understanding the cause

- **Notice** = becoming aware **through the senses** (sight, smell, sound)
- **Realize** = **understanding** what something means, processing consequences

> Notice is less cerebral — it’s external. Realize involves insightfulness — you process what it *means*.

sections.title: 5. Business Letter: Formal English  ★ Main topic
sections.content:
### Letter

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| A quien corresponda, | To whom it may concern, |
| Les escribo porque he sufrido daños personales a causa de un producto defectuoso fabricado por su empresa. | I am writing to you because I have suffered personal injury due to a defective product manufactured by your company. |
| Esta mañana decidí probar su nueva y "revolucionaria" cuchilla de afeitar de seis hojas (six-blade razor), The Six Drive. He sido un fiel cliente suyo durante más de 30 años y he empezado a dar por sentado no sólo el carácter innovador de sus productos, sino también su alta calidad. | This morning I decided to try out your new "revolutionary" six-blade razor, The Six Drive. I have been a loyal customer of yours for over 30 years and have started to take for granted not only the innovative nature of your products, but also their high quality. |
| Así que podrán imaginar mi decepción y enfado cuando, después de haberme afeitado, mi cara parecía como si hubiera sido atacada salvajemente por un gato psicópata. Cuando examiné la cuchilla con la que me había rasurado, vi que dos de las hojas estaban partidas por la mitad. Por culpa de estas hojas rotas tengo la cara cubierta de arañazos y tengo suerte de no haber sufrido lesiones mayores. Adjunto fotos de mi cara y de la cuchilla culpable. | So you will be able to imagine my disappointment and anger when, after shaving, my face looked as if it had been savagely attacked by a psychopathic cat. When I examined the blade I had shaved with, I found that two of the blades were broken in half. Due to these broken blades my face is covered in scratches and I am lucky not to have suffered more serious injuries. I enclose photos of my face and the offending blade. |
| ¿Qué piensan hacer para compensarme por este desafortunado suceso? | What do you intend to do to make up for this unfortunate incident? |
| Atentamente, | Yours sincerely, |

---

A complaint letter translated from Spanish, practising key formal English phrases.

---

### Key phrases and vocabulary

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| A quien corresponda | **To whom it may concern** |
| Defectuoso | **Defective** / **faulty** |
| Cliente (compra producto) | **Customer** |
| Cliente (compra servicio) | **Client** |
| Dar por sentado | **To take for granted** |
| Más de 30 años | **Over** 30 years *(more natural than “more than”)* |
| Probar algo nuevo | **To try out** |
| Intentar | **To try** |
| Compensar | **To compensate** / **to make up for** |
| Como si | **As if** |
| Arañazos | **Scratches** |
| Adjunto dentro del sobre | **Enclosed** |
| Adjunto al email | **Attached** |
| El culpable (un objeto) | **The offending** — *the offending blades* |

---

### Grammar notes

**Who vs. Whom:** Grammar books say use *whom* for objects, but in real life almost nobody does — except **“To whom it may concern.”**

**“Will can” does not exist →** use **“will be able to”:**
> *You’ll be able to imagine my anger.*

**Enclosed vs. Attached:**
- *Enclosed* = inside the envelope / embedded in the email body.
- *Attached* = a separate file annexed to the email (like a PDF).

**Customer vs. Client:**
- *Customer* = someone who buys a **product**.
- *Client* = someone who buys a **service**.

**Try vs. Try out:**
- *Try* = intentar (*I tried to climb the wall but I couldn’t.*)
- *Try out* = probar algo nuevo (*I decided to try out your new razor.*)

**Defective vs. Faulty:** both mean *defectuoso*. *Faulty* comes from *fault* (falta/defecto).

---

### Oversleep vs. Sleep in

| Expression | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **To oversleep** | Quedarse dormido — problem, unintentional | *I overslept and missed the bus.* |
| **To sleep in** | Dormir más — intentional, no problem | *Tomorrow I can sleep in — it's Sunday.* |

---

### Compromiso — False Friend ⚠️

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Tengo un **compromiso** (obligación) | I have a **commitment** *(not "a compromise")* |
| Hemos llegado a un **acuerdo** / punto medio | We've reached a **compromise** |

> *Compromise* = a mutual agreement where both sides give a little. *Commitment* = an obligation or promise.

---

### To merge / A merger

- **To merge** = fusionarse → *The two companies merged.*
- **A merger** = la fusión (de empresas) → *It took months to negotiate the merger.*

sections.title: 2. Work vs. Job / Layoff vs. Fired
sections.content:
### Work (uncountable) vs. Job (countable)

| Word | Type | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Work** | Uncountable noun / verb | *He loves his work. She works hard.* |
| **Job** | Countable noun | *He has two jobs.* |

- *He does good **work**.*
- *He has a good **job**.*
- *My friend has two **jobs** — one in an office, one in a restaurant.*

> **Works** (countable) = *obra* — literary or artistic:
> *The complete **works** of Shakespeare · **works** of poetry · a **work** of art*

---

### Layoff vs. Fired

| Expression | Spanish | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Laid off** | Despedido sin culpa propia | Economic reasons, redundancy — not your fault |
| **Fired** | Despedido con causa | Your fault — misconduct, theft, poor performance |

- *He got **laid off** because the economy went bad.*
- *He got **fired** because he was stealing from the company.*

---

### Industry vs. Sector

Both are correct, but **industry** is more common in everyday English:
- *I work in the financial **industry**.*
- *There have been massive layoffs in the tech **industry**.*

sections.title: 3. Mastering the Interrogative  ★ Main topic
sections.content:
Form a question by identifying the **question word**, then: **question word + auxiliary + subject + verb?**

> Give the statement → identify what information is being asked → build the question.

---

### Coca-Cola facts → questions

| Statement | Question |
|---|---|
| Coca-Cola was invented **in 1886**. | **When** was Coca-Cola invented? |
| The inventor was **John Pemberton**. | **Who** was the inventor of Coca-Cola? |
| The headquarters is **in Atlanta**. | **Where** is the headquarters of Coca-Cola? |
| The main ingredient is **carbonated water**. | **What** is the main ingredient in Coca-Cola? |
| The logo is **red and white**. | **What color** is the famous Coca-Cola logo? |
| Coca-Cola was first sold **at a pharmacy**. | **Where** was Coca-Cola first sold? |
| The company was founded by **Asa Candler**. | **Who** was the Coca-Cola company founded by? |
| Coca-Cola sponsors **the Olympic Games**. | **What** does Coca-Cola sponsor? |
| Coca-Cola owns the brand **Fanta**. | **What brand** does Coca-Cola own? |
| Coke had a giant failure with **New Coke**. | **What** did Coca-Cola have a giant failure with? |
| They introduced the contoured bottle **in 1915**. | **When** did they introduce the contoured bottle? |
| New Coke was introduced **in 1985**. | **When** did Coca-Cola introduce New Coke? |
| Coca-Cola Orange was introduced **in 2007**. | **When** did Coca-Cola introduce Coca-Cola Orange? |

sections.title: 4. Coca-Cola History & Vocabulary
sections.content:
### Key facts

- Invented in **1886** by **John Pemberton**, a pharmacist in **Atlanta**.
- Originally sold at **pharmacies** — carbonated water was believed to aid digestion.
- The Coca-Cola *company* was founded by **Asa Candler**, who built the bottling and distribution empire.
- The iconic **contoured bottle** was introduced in **1915**.
- **New Coke** launched in **1985** — a huge failure. After public backlash, the original was renamed **Coca-Cola Classic**.
- **Coca-Cola Orange** introduced in **2007**.
- Owns many brands including **Fanta** and various bottled water brands. Sponsors the **Olympic Games**.

---

### Names for soft drinks by region

| Region | Word |
|---|---|
| Canada | **Pop** |
| USA — Northeast (New York) | **Soda** |
| USA — South (Florida) | **Coke** *(used for any soft drink)* |
| Formal / universal | **Soft drink** |

> In the US South: *"What kind of Coke do you want?" "A Sprite."*

---

### Sweetener differences

| Region | Sweetener in regular Coke |
|---|---|
| USA | High fructose corn syrup |
| Europe | Sugar (beet sugar) |
| Mexico | Cane sugar *(Mexican Coke is popular in the US for its flavor)* |

sections.title: 5. Speculate & Forecast
sections.content:
### To speculate — especular

> To form opinions without firm evidence; to invest in hopes of profit.

| Example |
|---|
| I speculated on the stock market last year. |
| They have speculated about the reasons for the decision. |
| Are you speculating when you say that? |

> **Pronunciation:** unvoiced S — say **"speculate"**, not **"a-speculate"**.

---

### To forecast — prever

> To predict future events. Can be a **verb** or a **noun**.

| Example |
|---|
| They forecasted sales of over 3 million euros. |
| Economists have forecasted a rise in the stock market. |
| I'm forecasting a fall in sales this year. |
| Is it possible to correctly forecast a recession? |

> **A weather forecast** (noun) = el pronóstico del tiempo.

> **Prever** conjugation note: *prevé*, not *prevere*.

title: English with Kyle
topic: Quantifying Time: Since / Ago / For / During / While

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
**Translation practice from class**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Aléjate del vapor | Get away from the steam |
| Tiene una nariz tan grande | He has such a big nose |
| Es feo solo por fuera | He's only ugly on the outside |
| Está demasiado ocupado haciéndose rico | He's too busy getting rich |
| ¿Te importaría recoger tus zapatos? | Would you mind picking up your shoes? |
| La fecha de renovación se ha cambiado | The renewal date has been changed |

---

**Pry / Snoop / Nosy**

| Expression | Spanish | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **To be nosy** | Ser cotilla / curioso | Asks personal questions to gain info others may not want to share |
| **To pry into** | Entrometerse (con fuerza) | Stronger — forcing into someone's private life |
| **To snoop around** | Husmear / curiosear | Secretly acquiring info when someone is away |

> *To pry* also means to force something open physically: *He pried open the door.*

---

**So … that / Such … that**

| Pattern | Example |
|---|---|
| **so** + adjective (+ that) | His nose is **so** big that you can see it from space |
| **such a/an** + adjective + noun (+ that) | He has **such a** big nose that everyone notices |

---

**Too vs. Very**

- **Very** = mucho (neutral intensifier): *He is very busy.*
- **Too** = demasiado (excessive, implies a problem): *He's **too** busy to answer.*

> *He's too busy getting rich* — suggests it's excessive / a complaint.

---

**Would you mind + -ing?**

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Te importaría recoger tus zapatos? | Would you mind **picking up** your shoes? |
| ¿Te importaría cerrar la puerta? | Would you mind **closing** the door? |

> *Would you mind* is always followed by the **-ing** form.

sections.title: 2. Prepositions of Time: In / On / At
sections.content:
Think of a **triangle from broad to specific**: **in → on → at**

| Preposition | Used with | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **in** | months, seasons, years | *in June · in the summer · in 2020* |
| **on** | days of the week, specific dates | *on Monday · on the 23rd · on Christmas Day* |
| **at** | specific clock times | *at 8:30 · at noon · at midnight* |

---

### Exceptions

**At Christmas** vs. **On Christmas Day**

- *At Christmas* = the whole holiday period (roughly Dec 20 – Jan 6): *At Christmas I eat a lot.*
- *On Christmas Day* = the specific 25th of December: *On Christmas Day I'll be with my family.*

**In the morning / at night**

- We say **in the morning**, **in the afternoon**, **in the evening**
- But: **at night** *(exception — not "in the night", which sounds poetic / literary)*

| ✓ | ✗ |
|---|---|
| I'll see you in the morning | ~~I'll see you in the night~~ |
| I check emails at night | ~~I check emails in the night~~ |

sections.title: 3. Since — Desde  ★ Main topic
sections.content:
**Since** = *desde* — always followed by a **moment** in time.

> Whenever you use *since*, you will use a **perfect tense** (present perfect or past perfect).

---

### Basic use — present perfect

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Llevo sentado aquí desde las 8:30 | I've been sitting in this chair **since 8:30** |
| No le he visto desde entonces | I haven't seen him **since then** |
| Salió de la empresa en 2014; desde entonces solo le he visto una vez | She left the company in 2014; **since then**, I've only seen her once |
| Le conozco desde 2010 | I've known him **since 2010** |
| Nos conocimos en una fiesta y desde entonces estamos juntos | We met at a party and we've been together **ever since** |

---

### Since vs. For — common mistake ⚠️

**Since** + a moment in time: *since 8:30, since 2010, since last week*

**For** + a period of time: *for three years, for a long time*

| ✗ Common mistake | ✓ Correct |
|---|---|
| It's been three years that I **don't** play tennis | I **haven't** played tennis **for** three years |
| It's been three years that I don't play | It's been three years **since** I last played tennis |

> In Spanish you can use a negative (*hace tres años que no juego*), but in English — no negative.

---

### Since + ago (desde hace)

*Desde hace* = **since** + time + **ago** — or simply **for** + period:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Le conozco desde hace 16 años | I've known him **since 16 years ago** / I've known him **for 16 years** |
| Le conozco desde hace dos años | I've known him **since two years ago** |

---

### Since = "ya que" (causal)

*Since* can also express **reason** — like *ya que* or *dado que*:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ya que estás aquí, tomemos algo | **Since** you're here, let's have a beer |
| Como está lloviendo, quedémonos en casa | **Since** it's raining, let's stay at home |
| Dado que el tiempo será terrible, nos quedaremos | **Since** the weather's going to be terrible, we'll stay home |

---

### Superlatives: ever, not never ⚠️

- It's the worst movie I've **ever** seen. *(NOT "never seen" — you have seen it)*
- He was the strongest person I've **ever** met.
- It's the best film I will **ever** see. *(future: nothing will ever be better than this)*

sections.title: 4. Ago / For / During / From…to
sections.content:
### Ago — hace

Used with **simple past**. Equivalent of *hace* for completed actions.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Le vi hace cinco minutos | I saw him **five minutes ago** |
| Mi hermano me llamó hace una hora y media | My brother called me **an hour and a half ago** |

> **Ago** follows the time period: *two days ago, a week ago, three years ago.*

---

### For — durante / desde hace

Used with a **period** of time.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Hablé con ella durante una hora | I spoke to her **for an hour** |
| No he jugado al tenis en tres años | I haven't played tennis **for three years** |
| Le conozco desde hace 16 años | I've known him **for 16 years** |

> When *durante* refers to a **duration** (e.g. *una hora, dos días*), use **for** — not *during*.

---

### During — durante (+ noun/event)

*During* places an event **inside a period** — followed by a **noun**, not a duration.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Durante la película hablé con mi amigo | **During the movie**, I spoke to my friend |
| Durante la fiesta conocí a María | **During the party**, I met María |

| ✓ during + noun/event | ✓ for + duration |
|---|---|
| during the movie | for an hour |
| during the party | for three years |
| during the class | for a long time |

---

### From … to — desde … hasta

Used for a **defined period** you are **not currently inside**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Obama fue presidente desde 2009 hasta 2017 | Obama was president **from 2009 to 2017** |
| Ayer estuve hablando de 6 a 7 | Yesterday I was talking **from 6 to 7** |

> If you are **still inside the period**, use **since**: *Trump has been president **since** 2025.*

sections.title: 5. While / Before / After / Meanwhile
sections.content:
### While — mientras

*While* = *mientras* — followed by a **subject + verb** (unlike *during*, which takes a noun).

Often paired with the **past continuous** for an action in progress.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Mientras estaba en clase me llamó mi madre | **While I was in class**, my mother called me |
| Mientras hablaba contigo oí a mi vecino | **While I was talking to you**, I heard my neighbor |
| ¿Pasó algo mientras estaba fuera? | Did anything happen **while I was away**? |
| Disfrútalo mientras dure | Enjoy it **while it lasts** |
| No escribas mensajes mientras conduces | Don't write messages **while you drive** |

> *During* + noun · *While* + subject + verb

---

### Before / After — tres estructuras

| Pattern | Example |
|---|---|
| before/after + **noun** | I'll call you **after the meeting** |
| before/after + **gerund (-ing)** | I'll call you **after giving the presentation** |
| before/after + **subject + verb** | I called him **after he gave the presentation** |

---

### Meanwhile vs. In the meantime

topic: I don't think I will / Noun-based Adjectives / Compound Adjectives

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Los escoceses tienen un acento extraño | The Scottish have a strange accent |
| Tienen fama de ser tacaños | They're famous for being stingy / They have a reputation for being tight-fisted |
| Si fuera zurdo, podría hacerlo | If I were left-handed, I could do it |
| Esa gente es de mente muy estrecha | These people are very narrow-minded |
| Déjame que te releve | Let me take over for you |
| Creo que no lo oyeron | I don't think they heard |

---

### The + nationality adjective as a group noun

When a nationality word is an **adjective**, you can use *the* to refer to the whole group — no plural -s:

| Group | Adjective form (no -s) | Noun form |
|---|---|---|
| Escoceses | **The Scottish** have a strange accent | — |
| Chinos | **The Chinese** are consuming more technology | — |
| Españoles | **The Spanish** are improving their English | Spaniards / a Spaniard |
| Canadienses | ~~The Canadian~~ | **The Canadians** live in Canada |

> *Canadian* is not used as a group adjective noun — you need the noun: *the Canadians*.

---

### Famous for / Well-known for / Have a reputation for

All three collocations take **for** + gerund or noun:

- *They're **famous for** being stingy.*
- *They're **well-known for** being tight-fisted.*
- *They **have a reputation for** being stingy.*
- *Ávila is famous for its walls.*

---

### Like vs. As

| Expression | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **as** | Factual — it's true | *I work as a teacher.* |
| **like** | Metaphorical / comparison | *I work like a slave.* *(I'm not actually a slave)* |

sections.title: 2. "I don't think I will" — Negative Shift  ★ Main topic
sections.content:
In English, when *creo que no…* expresses negative belief, we make **the verb think negative**, not the subordinate clause.

> ✗ I think they didn't hear → ✓ **I don't think** they heard

This is called **negative raising** — the negative moves up to *think*.

---

### Examples

| Spanish | ✗ Direct | ✓ Natural English |
|---|---|---|
| Creo que no lo oyeron | I think they didn't hear | **I don't think** they heard |
| Creo que no importa | I think it doesn't matter | **I don't think** it mattered |
| Creo que él no lo quería decir | I think he didn't mean it | **I don't think** he meant it |
| Creo que no iré | I think I won't go | **I don't think** I'll go |
| Creo que no puedo ir a la fiesta | I think I can't go | **I don't think** I can go |
| Creo que no deberías hacer eso | I think you shouldn't do that | **I don't think** you should do that |
| Creo que no estarán allí | I think they won't be there | **I don't think** they'll be there |

---

### To make it — poder asistir / llegar a tiempo

*Make it* is a useful idiom for *poder ir / llegar a tiempo*:

| Example | Spanish |
|---|---|
| I don't think I'll **make it** to the party | Creo que no podré ir a la fiesta |
| I don't think I can **make it** | Creo que no puedo asistir |
| We're not going to **make it** | No vamos a llegar (a tiempo) |

sections.title: 3. Let vs. Allow
sections.content:
Both mean *dejar / permitir*, but the grammar differs:

| Verb | Structure | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **let** | let + person + **bare infinitive** (no *to*) | *My mother didn't let me drink beer.* |
| **allow** | allow + person + **to** + infinitive | *My mother didn't allow me to smoke.* |

> *Let me explain* ✓ — *Let me to explain* ✗

- *When I was young, my mother didn't **let** me drink beer.*
- *When I was young, my mother didn't **allow** me to smoke cigarettes.*

> **Allow** is slightly more formal. **Let** is more common in everyday speech.

sections.title: 4. Used to / Be used to / Get used to
sections.content:
Three different structures — easy to confuse:

| Structure | Meaning | What follows | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **used to** + infinitive | Solía (past habit, no longer true) | bare infinitive | *I used to drive a diesel car.* |
| **be used to** + noun/gerund | Estar acostumbrado a | noun or -ing | *I am used to the weather. / I'm used to living here.* |
| **get used to** + noun/gerund | Acostumbrarse (in progress) | noun or -ing | *I'm getting used to it.* |

---

**Examples of each:**

- *I used to play football every weekend.* *(ya no juego)*
- *I'm used to rainy days.* *(already accustomed)*
- *I'm used to experiencing a lot of rain.* *(gerund after be used to)*
- *I'm getting used to the weather here.* *(still adjusting)*

> **Get** here follows its pattern of *becoming*: get dirty, get wet, get strong → *get used to*.

sections.title: 5. Noun-based Adjectives (-y suffix)  ★ Second main topic
sections.content:
Many English adjectives are formed by adding **-y** to a noun. The result means "having the quality of that noun."

| Noun | Adjective | Spanish | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| water | **watery** | aguado | *The coffee was a bit watery.* |
| rain | **rainy** | lluvioso | *A very rainy day.* |
| spice | **spicy** | picante | *The food is very spicy.* |
| smell | **smelly** | oloroso / maloliente | *A smelly room.* |
| fruit | **fruity** | afrutado | *A very fruity flavor.* |
| flower | **flowery** | floreado | *A flowery scent.* |
| smoke | **smoky** | ahumado | *The room was very smoky.* |
| juice | **juicy** | jugoso | *A juicy steak.* |
| chalk | **chalky** | calcáreo | *A chalky texture.* |
| earth | **earthy** | terroso | *An earthy flavor — the potatoes taste of earth.* |
| wind | **windy** | ventoso | *It's a very windy day.* |
| storm | **stormy** | tormentoso | *Stormy weather ahead.* |

> **Pattern:** noun → add -y → adjective meaning "having the character of [noun]"
>
> Very common in English for describing taste, smell, weather, and texture.

sections.title: 6. Compound Adjectives & Hyphens
sections.content:
When **two or more words form a single adjective** before a noun, connect them with a **hyphen (-)** — a *guión medio*.

### Key examples from class

| Spanish | English compound adjective |
|---|---|
| Tacaño | **tight-fisted** |
| Zurdo | **left-handed** |
| Diestro | **right-handed** |
| De mente estrecha | **narrow-minded** |
| De cinco años | **five-year-old** |

---

### Rule: adjectives don't take plural in English

When a noun is used as part of a compound adjective, it stays **singular**, even if the meaning is plural:

- *a **five-year**-old boy* ✓ — NOT ~~a five-years-old boy~~ ✗
- *a **ten-minute** break* ✓ — NOT ~~a ten-minutes break~~ ✗

---

### Underscore vs. Hyphen

| Symbol | Name | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `-` | hyphen (*guión medio*) | compound adjectives, compound nouns |
| `_` | underscore (*guión bajo*) | email addresses, file names |

sections.title: 7. Picture Vocabulary — Two Women at a Well
sections.content:
Kyle showed a photo of two women getting water from a desert well — used to practice **present continuous** (live description) then **past continuous** (after the photo was gone).

### Vocabulary from the scene

| Word / phrase | Spanish | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| a **well** | un pozo | A hole in the ground with water |
| a **watering can** | una regadera | Container with a spout |
| a **bucket** | un cubo | Open container |
| a **water pump** | una bomba de agua | Device that pushes water up |
| to **pump** the water | bombear el agua | *She was pumping water into the can.* |
| a **shawl** | un chal | Cloth covering head and shoulders |
| **arid** | árido | Very dry — *a fairly arid environment* |
| **sparse** | escaso / esparcido | Few and spread out — *sparse bushes* |
| **dusty** | polvoriento | *A very dusty environment.* |
| to **bend over** | inclinarse | *She was bending over to fill her bucket.* |

> **Bend**: a slight curve. **Bend over**: to lean the body forward (inclinar el cuerpo).
>
> **Fold** (doblar completamente, e.g. paper) is different from **bend** (slight curve).

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No perdamos contacto con la realidad | Let's not lose touch with reality |
| No construyamos castillos en el aire | Let's not build castles in the air |
| Te pareces a tu madre (físicamente) | You look like your mother |
| Te pareces a tu madre/padre (carácter) | You take after your mother / your father |
| Ya aprenderás los secretos del oficio | You'll learn the tricks of the trade |
| La culpa fue de Pepe | It was Pepe's fault |
| No me eches la culpa | Don't blame me |
| ¿Te están dando mucha guerra? | Are they giving you a hard time? |
| Al contrario | On the contrary |
| No me costumbro (al clima) | I can't get used to it |

---

### Notes

- **Reality** — no article in English: *Let's not lose touch with **reality*** (not ~~the reality~~).
- **Castles in the air** — an idiom for unrealistic dreams or plans.
- **Tricks of the trade** — the skills and knowledge acquired through experience in a profession.
- **Hard time** — more native-sounding than *a lot of trouble*: *Are they giving you a hard time?*

sections.title: 2. "Way" as Amplifier  ★ Main topic
sections.content:
Use **way** before a comparative adjective/adverb or before *more/fewer/less* to mean *much more / by far*. It sounds natural and very native.

---

### Way + comparative adjective

| Example | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Nadal is **way better** at tennis than I am | much better |
| Madrid is **way bigger** than Salamanca | much bigger |
| This week is **way hotter** than last week | much hotter |
| He's **way smarter** than me | much smarter |
| Spain is **way better** at football than the US | much better |

---

### Way + more / fewer / less

| Example | Note |
|---|---|
| There are **way more** people in Madrid than in Soria | countable |
| I drank **way more** coffee today than yesterday | uncountable |
| Canada has **way more** space than Spain | uncountable |
| There are **way more** cars here than in Trujillo | countable |

> ⚠️ We say *way more*, never ~~way many~~.

---

### Way too + adjective/adverb

| Example | Meaning |
|---|---|
| It's **way too far** to walk | mucho demasiado lejos |
| It would take **way too long** | mucho demasiado tiempo |
| It's **way too hot** | hace un calor excesivo |
| He's **way too intelligent** to be in that class | demasiado inteligente |
| I'm **way too tired** | estoy agotadísimo |

---

### How to use it

- ✓ *That was way better than I expected.*
- ✓ *You'll sound way more native if you use this.*
- ✓ *I drank way more coffee than I should have.*
- ✗ ~~way many~~ — always use *way more* even with countables

sections.title: 3. "Way" — Direction & Manner
sections.content:
**Way** also means *direction*, *route*, or *manner*.

---

### Direction

| Expression | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Which way?** | ¿En qué dirección? | *Which way did he go?* |
| **On the way** | De camino | *We can talk about it on the way.* |
| **In the way** | En medio, obstruyendo | *There's a car in the way.* |
| **Out of the way** | Quítate/apártate | *Get out of the way!* |
| **I'm on my way** | Estoy de camino | *I'm on my way, see you soon.* |

> **Which** vs **What**: Use *which way* when the options are limited and visible (e.g. at an intersection). *Which* implies defined choices; *what* is open-ended.

---

### The way things stand / the way things are

> *The way things stand, I don't think it's a good idea.*
> = Tal y como están las cosas…

---

### Way = manner / method

> *I wouldn't do it **that way**.*
> *That's the best **way** to learn English.*
> *A lot of people have tried different **ways** of learning English.*

sections.title: 4. Blame · Fault · Guilty
sections.content:
Three related words about responsibility — each plays a different grammatical role.

| Word | Role | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **blame** | verb | *Don't blame me. / You're always looking for someone to blame.* |
| **fault** | noun | *It was Pepe's fault. / La culpa fue de Pepe.* |
| **guilty** | adjective | *He was found guilty of the crime.* |

---

### Examples

- *It was Pepe's fault* — la culpa fue de Pepe
- *Don't blame me* — no me eches la culpa
- *You're always looking for someone to blame* — siempre buscas a alguien a quien echarle la culpa
- *He was guilty of the crime* — era culpable del crimen

---

> The goal of the judicial system is to **blame** people who are **guilty**; their **fault** must be proven.

sections.title: 5. "Take After" vs "Look Like"
sections.content:
| Expression | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **look like** | Physical resemblance | *You look like your mother.* (te pareces físicamente) |
| **take after** | Character / behaviour | *You take after your father.* (te pareces en la forma de ser) |

---

### Key rules for *take after*

- Used **only with family members**: you take after your mother, father, grandfather…
- Refers to **character, behaviour, personality** — not physical appearance.
- ✓ *You take after your grandfather — you're both very patient.*
- ✗ ~~You take after your mother in looks~~ → say *you look like your mother* instead.

sections.title: 6. Get Used To / Be Used To (recap)
sections.content:
These came up in the warm-up (*no me costumbro*).

| **get used to** + noun/gerund | Acostumbrarse (proceso) | *I can't get used to the heat.* |
| **be used to** + noun/gerund | Estar acostumbrado | *I'm used to the cold.* |
| **used to** + infinitive | Pasado habitual (distinto) | *I used to live in Canada.* |

> *I can't get used to it* — no me costumbro (proceso de adaptación, aún no logrado)
> Before you can **be used to** something, you have to **get used to** it first.

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
Practice translating these Spanish sentences into English.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Hay una escasez de mano de obra cualificada en este país. | There's a shortage of skilled labor in this country. |
| No hay ni un solo ingeniero de caminos. | There's not even a single civil engineer. |
| Debería haber previsto ese problema. | You should have foreseen that problem. |
| Mándame un fontanero y un electricista. | Send me a plumber and an electrician. |
| El pobre hombre sufrió lesiones graves. | The poor man suffered serious injuries. |
| Tuvo varias costillas rotas. | He had several broken ribs. |
| Menos mal que estaba asegurado. | It's a good thing he was insured. |
| Abra el libro por la página cuarenta. | Open the book **to** page 40. |
| La letra de la canción. | The lyrics **to** the song. |
| El conductor estaba muerto de miedo. | The driver was scared to death. |

**Vocabulary notes:**

- **shortage** = escasez (emphasises lack; *falta* is more neutral)
- **skilled labor** = mano de obra cualificada
- **foresee / foreseen** = prever / previsto
- **plumber** = fontanero (silent B — P-L-U-M-B-E-R; possibly from Latin *plumbum* = lead, as pipes were once made of lead)
- **injury** = lesión (general); **wound** = herida (open cut); **bruise** = moratón
- **several** = varios, emphasising the quantity is large (vs *some* = algunos, neutral)

**Preposition challenge:**

- Open the book **to** page 40 — not *on* page 40.
- The lyrics **to** the song — not *of* the song (though *of* is not wrong, *to* is far more natural).

sections.title: 2. Miss vs Lose
sections.content:
Inspired by an old **Vaughan English** magazine from April 2006 with the headline:

> *"Missing Miss Loses the Plot"*

---

### TO MISS

**1. No aprovechar / no ver something** — to fail to catch, attend, or notice

| Example | Translation |
|---|---|
| I missed the bus, so I had to get a taxi. | Perdí el autobús, así que tuve que coger un taxi. |
| Due to the traffic, we missed the match. | Perdimos el partido debido al tráfico. |
| She missed three mistakes in the text. | Se le pasaron tres errores en el texto. |
| Excuse me, could you repeat? I missed that. | Perdón, ¿puedes repetir? No lo he entendido. |

**2. Miss out / FOMO**

- **To miss out** = perderse algo, no aprovechar una oportunidad.
- **FOMO** = *Fear Of Missing Out* — the anxiety of feeling you're missing something fun while others are enjoying it.

> *I don't want to go, but what if it's a lot of fun and I'm not there? I would miss out.*

**3. Echar de menos — to miss someone or something**

| Example | Translation |
|---|---|
| I miss my mother's cooking. | Echo de menos la cocina de mi madre. |
| I miss being young. | Echo de menos ser joven. |

> **Grammar tip:** After *miss*, use the **-ing** form of a verb, not the infinitive.
> - ✅ *I miss **being** with my friends.*
> - ❌ *I miss **to be** with my friends.*

---

### TO LOSE

**1. No encontrar — to be unable to find**

| Example | Translation |
|---|---|
| I've lost my keys. | He perdido mis llaves. |
| I lost the piece of paper you gave me. | He perdido el papel que me diste. |

**2. No ganar — to fail to win**

| Example | Translation |
|---|---|
| She always loses at cards. | Siempre pierde a las cartas. |

**3. Get lost = perderse**

> *When I first came to Madrid, I got lost a lot. It was pre-smartphone — I had an El Corte Inglés map in my pocket.*

**4. Lose the plot** = perder la chaveta; no entender qué está pasando

> *I've lost the plot.* = No entiendo qué está pasando aquí.

sections.title: 3. Can vs To Be Able To
sections.content:
Both express ability, but they behave differently across tenses.

| | Can | To be able to |
|---|---|---|
| Present | I **can** do it. | I **am able to** do it. |
| Past | I **could** do it. | I **was able to** do it. |
| Future | ❌ *will can* does not exist | I **will be able to** do it. |

**Key rule:** *Can* has no future form. Use *to be able to* whenever you need a future tense.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Podrá encontrarles? | Will she be able to find them? |
| ¿Por qué no podrá hacerlo? | Why won't he be able to do it? |

**Extra nuance:** *Can* often implies a **skill** or **knowledge**.

> *Can you read?* — implies knowing the skill of reading.

When *podrás* refers to a future possibility, you must switch to *will be able to*.

sections.title: 4. Mastering the Interrogative
sections.content:
Practice: given the **answer**, form the correct **question**.

| Answer | Question |
|---|---|
| The new law went into effect **last month**. | **When** did the new law go into effect? |
| The new rule has been in force **for a year and a half**. | **How long** has the new rule been in force? |
| You can stay here **as long as you want**. | **How long** can I stay here? |
| He broke it **last night**. | **When** did he break it? |
| They're expecting us **at 10 o'clock**. | **When** are they expecting us? |
| He's going to resign **later this year**. | **When** is he going to resign? |
| **This** book is mine. | **Whose** book is this? |
| **That** idea was Jennifer's. | **Whose** idea was that? |
| It depends **on you**. | **Who** does it depend on? |
| I used **the elevator on the left**. | **Which** elevator did you use? |
| The tank was emptied **by means of a pump**. | **How** was the tank emptied? |
| I got this shirt **in a small neighbourhood shop**. | **Where** did you get that shirt? |
| The bill was paid **on the 17th**. | **When** was the bill paid? |
| Nobody spoke to him because he was ill. | **Why** didn't anyone speak to him? |
| It stopped raining **shortly after lunch**. | **When** did it stop raining? |
| I used **a fire extinguisher** to put out the fire. | **What** did you use to put out the fire? |

---

**Grammar notes:**

**Whose — the noun always follows directly:**
- ✅ *Whose **book** is this?*
- ❌ *Whose is this book?* — wrong order.

**Nobody → Why didn't anyone…?**
When the statement uses *nobody / no one*, the question is more natural with a negative:
- ✅ *Why didn't **anyone** speak to him?*
- ⚠️ *Why did **no one** speak to him?* — grammatically possible but less common.

**Put out** = apagar (phrasal verb; the *out* signals extinction):
- *put out* the fire
- *blow out* the candles
- *smother out* a flame

**In effect / in force** — used interchangeably for laws and rules:
- *The law has been **in effect** / **in force** for two years.*

sections.title: 1. Vocabulary About Birth — Main Table
sections.content:
All vocabulary is practised inside full sentences using the **Ask Me** format.

| Word / Expression | Spanish | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **birth** (n.) | nacimiento | *The birth took place at 7 a.m.* |
| **due date** (n.) | fecha prevista / salir de cuentas | *My sister's due date is on the 7th of August.* |
| **to be due** (adj.) | estar previsto | *The baby is due on the 21st of December.* |
| **to have a nice ring to it** | sonar bien / ser eufónico | *Does the name Pamela have a nice ring to it?* |
| **to snort at sth** | resoplar / bufar ante algo | *Did you snort at his comment about the baby?* |
| **risky** (adj.) | arriesgado | *Is it risky to use too much medication for your baby?* |
| **at random** | aleatoriamente / al azar | *Will you pick your baby's name at random?* |

---

### Due Date vs To Be Due

**Due date** = noun. *My due date is the 7th of August.*

**To be due** = adjective use of *due*. *The baby is due on the 21st of December.*

> Both express a prediction / estimate, not a guarantee — that is why *due* (estar previsto) fits better than *will be born* (which sounds 100% certain).

---

### To Have a Nice Ring to It

Used when a name or word sounds pleasant, harmonious, or euphonic.

- *I really like the name Paloma. It has a nice ring to it.*
- Opposite: *That name does not have a very nice ring to it.*

> **Euphonious** (eufónico) = producing a soft, harmonious, pleasant sound — the adjective behind this expression.

---

### To Snort At

Literally: the nasal sound you make (bufar). Figuratively: to show **rejection or dissatisfaction** at a comment you do not like.

- *She snorted at his suggestion.* = resopló ante su sugerencia.

---

### At Random

= aleatoriamente, al azar.

- *They picked a name at random from the list.*
- *Do not choose at random — think carefully!*

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
Sentences translated from Spanish to English in today's warm-up.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No camines tan rápido. | **Don't walk so fast.** |
| Se tardan 10 minutos en cruzar el río. | **It takes 10 minutes to cross the river.** |
| No íbamos rápido cuando ocurrió. | **We weren't going fast when it happened.** |
| ¿Habrá examen mañana? | **Will there be an exam tomorrow?** |
| Hoy en día, la ropa no tiene que hacer juego. | **Nowadays, clothes don't have to match.** |
| Fui corriendo detrás de ella. | **I ran after her.** |
| La alcancé en la esquina. | **I caught up with her at the corner.** |
| Tropecé con Juan en el metro. | **I bumped into / ran into Juan on the subway.** |
| Nos quedamos sin gasolina. | **We ran out of gasoline.** |
| Desenchúfalo antes de repararlo. | **Unplug it before fixing it.** |
| Dan por sentado que estamos de acuerdo. | **They take for granted that we agree.** |
| Quiero desearte mucha suerte. | **I want to wish you the best of luck.** |
| Vaya golpe de suerte. | **What a stroke of luck.** |

---

### Key Notes

**Preposition + gerund:** After a preposition, use *-ing*. → *before fixing it* (not *before to fix it*).

**Nowadays** = these days (all one word, with the A in the middle).

**To match** = hacer juego, combinar (colours, clothes). ≠ *to fit* (quedar bien de talla).

**To agree** = estar de acuerdo. This verb has no direct equivalent in Spanish — it must be expressed with a verb. *I agree. Do you agree?*

**Advice** is uncountable → *three pieces of advice* / *three tips* (not *three advices*).

**Tip** has three meanings: *propina* / *consejo* / *la punta*. → The tip of the iceberg.

---

### Phrasal Verbs: run into · bump into · come across

| Expression | Meaning | Use with |
|---|---|---|
| **run into** / **bump into** | tropezar con alguien (by chance) | people |
| **come across** | encontrar algo (by chance) | things |

- *I ran into Juan on the metro.* → met someone unexpectedly.
- *I came across some old photos.* → found something unexpectedly.

sections.title: 2. Regular Verb Pronunciation — Three Rules
sections.content:
Regular verbs in English follow three pronunciation rules for the past tense **-ed** ending.

---

### Rule 1 — Verbs ending in **T** or **D**: add an extra syllable **/ɪd/**

The -ed is pronounced as a separate syllable.

| Infinitive | Past | Example |
|---|---|---|
| last | **lasted** | The game lasted two hours. |
| decide | **decided** | They decided to go home. |
| visit | **visited** | I visited my parents last month. |

---

### Rule 2 — Verbs ending in **K, F, P, SH, CH, S**: add **/t/** sound (no extra syllable)

| Infinitive | Past | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ask | **asked** | Alberto asked me a question. |
| help | **helped** | We helped each other. |
| wash | **washed** | They washed their hands. |
| laugh | **laughed** | She laughed at the joke. |
| kiss | **kissed** | He kissed. |
| check | **checked** | I checked the answer. |

> Common mistake: saying *asked* as two syllables. It is one syllable: *asked* /æskt/.

---

### Rule 3 — All other endings: add **/d/** sound (no extra syllable)

| Infinitive | Past | Example |
|---|---|---|
| happen | **happened** | Something happened at work. |
| arrive | **arrived** | Jessica arrived last night. |
| call | **called** | The client called. |
| smile | **smiled** | The baby smiled at me. |
| prepare | **prepared** | They prepared the presentation well. |
| change | **changed** | Everything changed. |

---

### D Pronunciation — English vs Spanish

In English, the tongue **never comes out past the teeth** with the letter D. In Spanish, the D at the end of a word (e.g. *dedo*) causes the tongue to stick out — this does **not** happen in English.

Practice: *decided · did · David decided · Don does the dishes*

sections.title: 3. I Don't Think I Can
sections.content:
In Spanish **creo que no** → in English the negative moves to *think*.

| ❌ Common mistake | ✅ Correct |
|---|---|
| I think I can't go. | **I don't think I can go.** |
| I think they won't be there. | **I don't think they'll be there.** |
| I think they didn't hear it. | **I don't think they heard it.** |

**Rule:** Move the negative to the verb *think* — don't negate the second verb.

More examples:
- *Creo que no estarán allí.* → **I don't think they'll be there.**
- *Creo que no lo oyeron.* → **I don't think they heard it.**
- *Creía que no importaba.* → **I didn't think it mattered.**

sections.title: 4. Fewer · Less / Not As Many · As
sections.content:
Two ways to make a negative comparison in English.

| Structure | Use with | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **fewer** + noun | countable nouns | There are fewer cars in Palencia than in Valencia. |
| **less** + noun | uncountable nouns | There is less rain in Valladolid than in Santiago. |
| **not as many** + noun + **as** | countable nouns | There are not as many cars in Palencia as there are in Valencia. |
| **not as much** + noun + **as** | uncountable nouns | There is not as much rain in Valladolid as there is in Santiago. |

> *Not as many / not as much* is more common in everyday speech than *fewer / less*.

---

### Pattern

**Countable:** *There are not as many [noun] in X as there are in Y.*

**Uncountable:** *There is not as much [noun] in X as there is in Y.*

When using *as*, use it **twice** — once before the noun and once before the comparison.

---

### Examples from Class

- There are not as many orange trees in Catalonia as there are in Valencia.
- There are not as many traffic lights in my hometown as there are in Madrid.
- There is not as much oil in Spain as in Saudi Arabia.
- I don't earn as much money as Paul McCartney.
- There are not as many dialects in North America as there are in Africa.
- There is not as much rain in Valladolid as there is in Santiago.

sections.title: 5. Irregular Verbs — Simple Past
sections.content:
Drill: *Every day I [verb]… yesterday I [past].*

| Infinitive | Simple Past | Sample sentence |
|---|---|---|
| send | **sent** | Yesterday I sent a letter to my friend. |
| sit | **sat** | Yesterday I sat in this chair for six hours. |
| sleep | **slept** | Yesterday I slept in my bed. |
| speak | **spoke** | Yesterday I spoke about verbs. |
| spend | **spent** | Yesterday I spent money at the supermarket. |
| stand | **stood** | Yesterday I stood on the street corner waiting for a taxi. |
| steal | **stole** | They stole my money. |
| take | **took** | Yesterday I took the bus. |
| teach | **taught** | Yesterday I taught the class. (T-A-U-G-H-T → /tɔːt/) |
| tell | **told** | Yesterday I told the story. |
| think | **thought** | Yesterday I thought about it. |
| throw | **threw** | Yesterday I threw the ball. |
| understand | **understood** | Yesterday I understood the lesson. |
| wear | **wore** | Yesterday I wore a jacket. |
| win | **won** | Yesterday I won the match. |
| write | **wrote** | Yesterday I wrote a message. |
| become | **became** | Yesterday I became a better speaker. |
| begin | **began** | The class began at six. |
| break | **broke** | Yesterday I broke a world record. |
| build | **built** | Yesterday I built something new. |

---

### Steal vs Rob

**To rob** → used with people or places (the victim or location).
**To steal** → used with the thing that is taken.

| Sentence | Explanation |
|---|---|
| They **robbed** the bank. | The bank was the target. |
| They **stole** the money. | The money was taken. |
| They **robbed** me. | I was the victim. |
| They **stole** my wallet. | My wallet was the thing taken. |

> **Rule:** People get **robbed**. Things get **stolen**.

A **robbery** = *un robo*. → *There was a robbery. What did they steal?*

You cannot say *they stole me* — that would mean kidnapping.

sections.title: 6. Another · Other · The Other
sections.content:
Three related words that Spanish speakers often confuse.

---

### another (singular)
= one additional / one more (*un otro* / *uno más*)

Used with singular countable nouns. Means there is at least one more of something.

- *Would you like **another** beer?*
- ***Another** opportunity will come.*
- *I'm looking for **another** idea.*
- *Can't you find **another** solution?*

---

### other (plural)
= the plural of *another*

- ***Other** opportunities will come.*
- *I'm looking for some **other** ideas.*
- *Can't you find **other** solutions?*

---

### the other (singular) / the other ones · the others (plural)
= *el otro / los otros* — refers to a **specific** remaining item or items.

- *Give me **the other** book.* (Dame el otro libro.)
- *Where are **the other ones**?* (¿Dónde están los otros?)
- ***The others** are waiting.* (Los otros están esperando.)

---

### Summary

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Dame **otro** libro. (one more) | Give me **another** book. |
| Dame **el otro** libro. (the specific other one) | Give me **the other** book. |
| Dame **los otros** libros. (the specific others) | Give me **the other** books. |
| Quiero **otros** libros. (some different ones) | I want **other** books. |

sections.title: 7. Present Perfect — I've Never…
sections.content:
Practice: answering *When did you last…?* with the **present perfect**.

**Pattern:** *When did you last [infinitive]…?* → *I have never [past participle]…*

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| When did you last **win** an archery contest? | I have never **won** an archery contest. |
| When did you last **write** a letter to the president of Japan? | I've never **written** a letter to the president of Japan. |
| When was the last time you **did** something for the Zambian ambassador? | I've never **done** anything for the Zambian ambassador. |
| When was the last time you **became** ill from eating almonds? | I have never **become** ill from eating almonds. |
| When did you last **catch** a train to Copenhagen? | I've never **caught** a train to Copenhagen. |
| When was the last time a Rolls Royce **cost** less than a refrigerator? | A Rolls Royce has never **cost** less than a refrigerator. |
| When did you last **drive** my car? | I have never **driven** your car. |
| When did you last **drink** 10 litres of water in a day? | I've never **drunk** 10 litres of water in a day. |
| When did you last **have** lunch with the president of Turkey? | I've never **had** lunch with the president of Turkey. |
| When did you last **deal** with an Arab stockbroker? | I've never **dealt** with an Arab stockbroker. |

> Note: *When did you last [verb]?* uses the **infinitive**. *When was the last time you…?* uses the **simple past**.

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
Sentences translated from Spanish to English in today's warm-up.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ojalá todo estuviera automatizado. | **I wish everything were automated.** |
| Las máquinas no se declaran en huelga. | **Machines don't go on strike.** |
| Exigen más dinero y menos trabajo. | **They demand more money and less work.** |
| Cualquier subida de salario está supeditada a un aumento en la productividad. | **Any wage increase will be tied to an increase in productivity.** |
| Sería un sueño hecho realidad. | **It would be a dream come true.** |
| Hacen lo que les dicen sin rechistar. | **They do what they're told without saying a word.** |
| Desenchúfalo antes de repararlo. | **Unplug it before repairing it.** |
| Déjame que te dé un consejo. | **Let me give you a piece of advice.** |

---

### Key Notes

**I wish + were (subjunctive):** Use *were* (not *was*) after *I wish* — this is the subjunctive mood.
- *I wish everything **were** automated.* ✅
- ~~I wish everything **was** automated.~~ ❌

**If only** works the same way as *I wish* but sounds more poetic:
- *If only everything were automated.*

**Advice is uncountable:**
- ✅ *Let me give you some advice.*
- ✅ *Let me give you a piece of advice.*
- ❌ *Let me give you an advice.*

**Rechistar** → *without saying a word* / *without complaining* / *without whining*

**Supeditada a** → *tied to* / *linked to* / *conditional on*

---

### Phrasal Verb: To Break In

**To break something in** = get something accustomed to use for the first few times.

- *I had to break in my new baseball glove.*
- *These new shoes need to be broken in.*
- *To break in a horse* = domar un caballo.

Note: **Estrenar** in English:
- Film/event → *to premiere*, *to debut*
- Clothes/shoes → *to wear for the first time*
- Shoes/gloves → *to break in* (phrasal verb)

sections.title: 2. How About · Shall · Let's
sections.content:
Three structures to **propose or suggest** something for the future.

---

### How About

Two forms:

| Pattern | Example |
|---|---|
| **How about** + *-ing* | How about going to the cinema? |
| **How about** + subject + infinitive | How about we go to the cinema? |

---

### Shall

**Only used in first person** (I / we) — never second or third.

| Pattern | Example |
|---|---|
| **Shall I** + infinitive | Shall I open the window? |
| **Shall we** + infinitive | Shall we go to the cinema? |

> ❌ *Shall you fix it?* / *Shall he come?* — NOT correct.

---

### Let's

Used in the **affirmative** (not interrogative like *shall*).
- *Let's go to the cinema.* (= Let us go…)

---

### Comparison — All Four Structures

| Structure | Example |
|---|---|
| How about + *-ing* | How about going to the cinema? |
| How about + subject + infinitive | How about we go to the cinema? |
| Shall we…? | Shall we go to the cinema? |
| Let's… | Let's go to the cinema. |
| Do you feel like…? | Do you feel like going to the cinema? |

---

### Practice Conversions

| Base | How about (*-ing*) | Shall we…? |
|---|---|---|
| buy a new one | How about buying a new one? | Shall we buy a new one? |
| fix the system | How about fixing the system? | Shall we fix the system? |
| stay at home | How about staying at home? | Shall we stay at home? |
| drive my car | How about driving my car? | Shall we drive my car? |

---

### Future Forms — Quick Overview

| Form | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| will | prediction, spontaneous decision | It will rain tomorrow. |
| going to | planned intention | I'm going to eat chicken tonight. |
| Present continuous | fixed arrangement | I'm eating chicken tonight. |
| Present simple | scheduled/timetabled event | I fly to Barcelona on Saturday. |
| How about / Shall / Let's | proposal / suggestion | Shall we go? |

sections.title: 3. Expressions of Frustration
sections.content:
Ways to say **estar harto / estar hasta las narices** in English.

---

### To be fed up with

*Estar harto de alguien/algo.*

- *I'm fed up with his loud music.*
- *She's getting fed up with the noise.*
- *We all got fed up with the weather.*

> ✅ Always followed by **with**.

---

### To get on one's nerves

*Poner los nervios de punta / sacar de quicio.*

- *He gets on my nerves.*
- *The loud music is getting on my nerves.*
- *Has the new boss started getting on his nerves yet?*

> ✅ No *with* — just the object pronoun.

---

### To drive someone up the wall

*Sacar a alguien de quicio / volverle loco.*

- *He drives me up the wall.*
- *The loud music is driving me up the wall.*
- *His bad habits drove her up the wall.*
- *Those new neighbours have already driven them up the wall.*

---

### To be sick and tired of

*Estar hasta la coronilla de.*

- *I'm sick and tired of the heat.*
- *She got sick and tired of me staying out so late.*
- *He never gets sick and tired of watching football.*

---

### Can't stand

*No aguantar / no soportar.*

- *I can't stand him.*
- *I can't stand the noise.*

> ✅ No *with* after *stand*.

---

### Summary Table

| Expression | Español | Followed by |
|---|---|---|
| be fed up **with** | harto de | with + noun/*-ing* |
| get on one's nerves | poner los nervios | direct object |
| drive someone up the wall | sacar de quicio | direct object |
| be sick and tired **of** | hasta la coronilla de | of + noun/*-ing* |
| can't stand | no soportar | direct object |

---

### Also useful

- *I'm fed up with putting up with my brother.* — *aguantar* = **to put up with** / **to stand** / **to bear**

sections.title: 4. Prepositions of Place
sections.content:
Prepositions describing where an object is in relation to a box.

| Preposition | Spanish | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **in** | dentro de | inside the box |
| **on** / **on top of** | encima de (tocando) | resting on the surface |
| **under** / **below** | debajo de | under the box |
| **next to** / **beside** | al lado de | touching or very close |
| **near** / **close to** | cerca de | close but not touching |
| **above** | por encima (sin tocar) | above but not touching |
| **over** | sobre / por encima | above (can also mean covering) |
| **between** | entre (dos) | between two objects |
| **among** | entre (varios) | among many objects |
| **behind** | detrás de | at the back |
| **in front of** | delante de | at the front |
| **far from** | lejos de | at a distance |
| **against** | contra (tocando) | touching the side of |

---

### Key Rules

**Near vs Near to:**
- ✅ *The ball is near the box.*
- ❌ *The ball is near to the box.*
- *Near to* is NOT used — just *near*.

**Above vs Over:**
- *Above* = strictly higher, not touching.
- *Over* = above, and can imply covering or crossing.

**Under vs Below:**
- Both mean beneath, but *below* is more about level/position on a scale.
- *Under the box* = directly beneath it.

sections.title: 1. Goal of This Class
sections.content:
This Friday class focuses on **natural reactions** — the automatic responses native speakers use in everyday conversation.

> We often learn to *produce* language (build sentences) but rarely practice *reacting* to what others say. This class fills that gap.

The four reaction categories practised today:

| Category | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Understanding** | Show you have understood |
| **Agreement** | Show you agree |
| **Doubt** | Express uncertainty |
| **Thinking** | Buy time before answering |

sections.title: 2. Showing Understanding
sections.content:
When someone explains something and you want to show you have understood:

| Expression | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Makes sense** | Drop *it / that* — more natural than *it makes sense* |
| **I get it** | Very common, casual |
| **Fair enough** | Accepting their reason as valid |
| **I see** | Simple acknowledgement |
| **Got it** / **Ah, got it** | Signals you have just understood |

**Example:** *"I was not at the meeting — I was not feeling well."*
→ *Makes sense · Fair enough · Got it*

sections.title: 3. Showing Agreement
sections.content:
When you fully agree with what someone said:

| Expression | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Absolutely** | Strong, enthusiastic agreement |
| **For sure** | Casual, confident agreement |
| **Couldn't agree more** | Emphatic — you agree 100% |
| **Totally** | Informal, very common |
| **Definitely** | Clear, confident agreement |
| **Exactly** | You think exactly the same |

**Example:** *"Sleeping eight hours a day is fantastic."* → agree
→ *For sure · Couldn't agree more · Totally*

sections.title: 4. Expressing Doubt
sections.content:
When you are not sure or cannot give a definite answer:

| Expression | Notes |
|---|---|
| **It depends** | The answer varies by circumstances |
| **I'm not sure** | Simple uncertainty |
| **Maybe** | Possibility, but no commitment |
| **Hard to say** | Difficult to give a clear answer |
| **I'm not convinced** | You have some doubts |

**Example:** *"Will AI replace teachers?"* → doubt
→ *It depends · Hard to say · I'm not convinced*

sections.title: 5. Buying Time to Think
sections.content:
When you need a moment before answering:

| Expression | Notes |
|---|---|
| **That's a good question** | Buys time while sounding engaged |
| **Honestly...** | Signals a thoughtful, genuine answer |
| **Let me think...** | Direct — you need a moment |
| **I've never thought about that** | Shows the question caught you off guard |
| **Off the top of my head...** | Giving an immediate, unpolished answer |

**Example:** *"What's your dream job?"* → think
→ *That's a good question · Let me think · Off the top of my head...*

opts: Off the top of my head...
qs.ans: Off the top of my head...

Someone proposes an idea and you agree 100%. Which expression shows the STRONGEST agreement?
